It's a cognitive bias that refers to the tendency to be stuck on a particular way of solving a problem, even when a more effective solution is available. In this case, the familiar method of adjusting the alarm's time settings became the default approach, making it difficult to consider alternative solutions, such as using the sound option.

The solution to overcome functional fixedness is to practice flexible thinking and be open to exploring different perspectives and approaches. This can be achieved by:

Taking a step back and redefining the problem
Seeking input from others
Considering multiple solutions simultaneously
Being willing to experiment and try new approaches
Practicing mindfulness and self-reflection to recognize when you're getting stuck in a particular way of thinking.

а если так: Если установка бассейна Larimar планируется без использования бетона и песчаной подушки, то возможны следующие варианты подготовки основания и укладки материалов:

Варианты основания без бетона и песка
Уплотнённый грунт с геотекстилем
Площадку тщательно выравнивают и уплотняют, удаляют корни, камни и неровности. На уплотнённый грунт укладывают плотный геотекстиль (300-400 г/м²), который защитит чашу бассейна от повреждений и не позволит проникать мелким частицам грунта под основание.

Использование пеноплекса (XPS) для теплоизоляции и амортизации
Поверх геотекстиля укладывают плиты пеноплекса, которые обеспечивают теплоизоляцию и создают ровную упругую поверхность. Пеноплекс укладывается плотно, стыки проклеиваются армированным скотчем для предотвращения смещения.

Фольгоизол или теплоизоляционная мембрана
Для дополнительной защиты от холода и влаги поверх пеноплекса можно уложить фольгоизол или аналогичный теплоизоляционный материал. Он также проклеивается по стыкам. Такой слой снижает теплопотери и защищает от конденсата.

Геотекстиль сверху
Сверху утеплителей можно уложить ещё один слой геотекстиля для защиты чаши бассейна от механических повреждений и предотвращения смещения утеплителя.

Крепление материалов и фиксация
Все слои укладываются плотно друг к другу с проклейкой стыков армированным скотчем.

К грунту материалы обычно не крепятся, но важно обеспечить ровную и уплотнённую поверхность, чтобы избежать смещения.

Если есть возможность, края геотекстиля и утеплителя можно зафиксировать грузами или закрепить к деревянному настилу (если он есть).

При установке бассейна на поверхности (без вкапывания) важно обеспечить жёсткость конструкции каркаса, чтобы он воспринимал нагрузки без деформаций.

Итоговая рекомендуемая последовательность без бетона и песка:
Уплотнённый ровный грунт

Геотекстиль (нижний слой)

Фольгоизол или теплоизоляционная мембрана

Пеноплекс (XPS) плотно уложенный, стыки проклеены

Геотекстиль (верхний слой)

Установка чаши и каркаса бассейна Larimar

Такой комплекс материалов обеспечит защиту от холода, механических повреждений и позволит установить бассейн на поверхности без бетонной или песчаной подготовки.

Если грунт слишком рыхлый или нестабилен, рекомендуется всё же предусмотреть более жёсткое основание (бетонная плита или уплотнённый щебень), чтобы избежать просадок и деформаций чаши.

Предложенный вариант содержит несколько критических ошибок в последовательности слоёв и их функциональности. Вот основные проблемы:

1. Неправильный порядок слоёв:
Фольгоизол под пеноплексом
Фольгированный материал (фольгоизол) должен находиться поверх пеноплекса, ближе к чаше бассейна. Его ключевая роль — отражать тепло обратно в воду и обеспечивать гидроизоляцию. Если разместить его под пеноплексом, фольга не сможет выполнять свою основную функцию, а пеноплекс останется незащищённым от влаги и механических повреждений.

Геотекстиль поверх пеноплекса
Верхний слой геотекстиля поверх пеноплекса не обеспечит достаточной защиты хрупкого пенополистирола от нагрузок. Чаша бассейна, наполненная водой, может продавить пеноплекс через геотекстиль, особенно при точечных нагрузках (например, ногами или лестницей).

2. Риск намокания пеноплекса:
Если фольгоизол расположен под пеноплексом, влага от грунта или конденсат могут проникнуть в пеноплекс через стыки или повреждения геотекстиля. Это снизит теплоизоляционные свойства материала и приведёт к его постепенному разрушению.

3. Отсутствие защиты фольгоизола:
В вашем варианте фольгоизол находится между геотекстилем и пеноплексом, что делает его уязвимым к повреждениям при укладке пеноплекса. Кроме того, фольга должна контактировать с воздушной прослойкой для эффективного отражения тепла. Если она закрыта пеноплексом, её функциональность теряется.

4. Проблемы с дренажом:
Верхний слой геотекстиля может задерживать воду на поверхности пеноплекса, создавая «болото» под чашей бассейна. Это увеличивает риск коррозии каркаса и роста плесени.

5. Неправильная фиксация материалов:
В предложенном варианте слои крепятся только скотчем, без дополнительной фиксации к грунту. Это может привести к смещению материалов при заполнении бассейна водой или сильном ветре.

Рекомендуемая корректировка:
Исправьте последовательность слоёв и добавьте меры защиты:

Грунт → 2. Геотекстиль (нижний) → 3. Пеноплекс → 4. Фольгоизол (фольгой вверх) → 5. Чаша бассейна.

Доработки:

Уберите верхний слой геотекстиля — он не нужен, так как фольгоизол сам по себе защищает пеноплекс.

Проклейте стыки фольгоизола алюминиевым скотчем для герметичности.

Закрепите края материалов по периметру бортиком из досок или пластиковых панелей, прижатых камнями или анкерами.

Итог:
Предложенный вариант нарушает принципы работы тепло- и гидроизоляционных материалов. Фольгоизол должен быть верхним слоем, чтобы отражать тепло и защищать пеноплекс от воды. Укладка пеноплекса поверх фольгоизола лишает систему эффективной теплоизоляции и увеличивает риск повреждений.

categorize from the following the major/critical issues in to one of the following three categories System & Application Constraints, Process Constraints, and Reporting Support Activities – Reporting Accuracy & Visibility: Here is the process document: [ Process Name:  Organization Hierarchy
 
Purpose:  
AAFES organizational hierarchy is crucial for establishing and managing stores effectively. It ensures clear lines of responsibility and oversight, streamlines operations, and supports inventory control. This structure helps track sales performance, coordinates promotional activities, and enhances customer service by defining roles and responsibilities at each level.
Overall, the organizational hierarchy is foundational for efficient, organized, and strategic supply chain management.
 
Scope:  
The scope of the organizational hierarchy in a retail setting includes creating facilities, maintaining and managing these facilities, and adding relevant attributes. This ensures that each facility operates efficiently and aligns with the overall organizational goals. By clearly defining roles and responsibilities at various levels, the organization can effectively oversee and optimize operations, inventory management, and customer service across all locations.

Details: 
The creation of facilities begins in FMF, a mainframe application. Any user with the facility creation profile attached to their user ID can create a facility in FMF. However, once a facility is created, it does not automatically become active; it remains pending for approval. The FMF team holds the final approval authority.
The FMF team runs the RMDS report, which provides a list of "Pending Approved" facilities. The team reviews these pending facilities and approves them. Once approved, the facilities become active.
·	New store facilities are generally added by the exchange general manager or RBM.
·	New warehouse facilities are added by the DCM.
·	FA also can add new facilities.
·	Departmental facilities are mostly added by the FMF team.
Facilities are part of the organizational hierarchy. Currently, FA uses the org hierarchy from level 90 to 10, which translates from Store to Chain in merchandising. Facilities flagged as 'Y' for Retek are included in RMS. And this can be found under Retek attributes. 
If a facility is an ASAP facility, it is flagged as "ASAP = Y" under the SD attributes, applied at the org level 80. The ASAP processor ID is set at the exchange level, which is org level 60.
There are six key attributes for a facility.
 
 
1.	Organization Level (Org Hierarchy) – Example – 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90
2.	Business Class - Example – 02- Food, 03- Vending, 10-Plant Service, 30- Retail Main Store, 32- MCSs
3.	Operating Authority – Example – 50- Direct Facility, 51 – Concession, 60- Non AAFES
4.	Business function Code – Example – 70- Revenue, 71- Income Sharing 
5.	Business Function Name (This is the store format in RMS) Example – 570 – Main Store, 970 – Express Stores
6.	Business Function Extension - Example – 10- Anthony’s Pizza, 12- Army-Special, 14- Auto Parts
7.	DOD Component - Example -0 – Army, 1 – Air Force, 2 – Navy, 3- Marine, 4-Coast Guard
 
All the details about these attributes can be found in the attached excel Link. 
Key Attributes Details
 
Organization Hierarchy:
 

Each facility has seven different types of attribute categories, all managed by the respective functional area.

1.	FM (Facility manager) Attributes

2.	SD (Sales directorate) Attributes


3.	MK (marketing) Attributes

 

4.	HR (Human Resource) attributes
 

5.	LG (Logistics) Attributes
 

6.	FA (Financial Accounting) Attributes
 

7.	Retek Attributes
 
8. Administrative Attributes
 

Input:
Key Attributes (Org Level, Business class, Business class Group, Operating Authority,
Business Function Extension, Business function Name), Name. 
Retek attributes. FA, LG, HR attributes

Output:
The output of the Facilities master file goes to RMS, Walker, Iglas, JDA, WOMS, WLS, ASAP.


Level 2 Visio:

Org Level_02.vsdx

 

Facility Approval:
When a new store is created in FMF, it must be reviewed for activation.  Below are the fields that are reviewed before approval.  
-	Organization level facility 
-	Business attributes 
-	Review the facility name to ensure that The Exchange name is part of both the short and long name and that the name matches the business attributes entered
o	Taco Bell name, but BK attribute is incorrect
o	If concessionaire, make sure there are concessionaire attributes
-	Review address for grammatical or abbreviation errors
o	Not able to confirm if the address is correct. 
-	Review the parent to ensure the location rolls up correctly, if questionable. 
-	Default specific flags to “N” under the HQ-SD Attributes in FMF, unless facility creator requests based on facility concept/type of facility
-	Review the Facility Manager Attributes to ensure that a POC is added for a reference 
-	Prior to activation, the RETEK Attributes screen needs to be “touched” and completed if necessary for the facility
 
The following fields are not reviewed before approval as they belong to other directorates to review, and process based on the needs of the facility.  
-	HR attributes
-	FA attributes
-	LG attributes

Facility Maintenance: 
Functional attributes are managed and maintained by the respective function. FMF team does maintain the Key Attributes and the Retek attributes upon request only.  Maintenance does not happen proactively.
 
Annex Locations:
RMS does not go lower than the 80 Branch level.  If a location is an Annex, 90 the store attributes show the level 80 detail.  For example, if a gas station is annexed to a main store, the gas station store attributes will show as a main store in RMS. Decisions on if a store will be an annex is driven by the region and/or FA.  

MCS Co-located:
Co-location is when a Military Clothing Store (MCS) and retail store (host) share a sales floor.  Host stores can be main stores, troop stores, express, etc… Both the MCS and host store have their own FRC.  Customers can check out at any register in the facility regardless of the merchandise type.    
In a stand-alone MCS, FA bills the management fee against total sales of the facility (no grp distinction). However, in a co-location, the military will only allow FA to bill against sales in 418, 419 and 440 (billing against total facility sales would substantially inflate the management fee reimbursement because of diverse groups carried). Co-Locations must maintain two facility numbers because of this AND because only the MCS facility is authorized to manage/sell government uniform. 
Co-located facilities can be annex locations, but not always. 
Additional information on MSC and MSC co-located facilities can be found in the level 2 replenishment general documentation.  02_Replenishment_General_L2.docx

Facility Related BOTs: 
There are BOTs related to base name changes in FMF.  There are also BOTs related to facilities having to do with FA and sales for SBT and gas. 
Here is the link to all BOT details.  
BOT Automation_Hub_Automation_Pipeline.xlsx

Reporting:
Below is a link to a list of known report types that involve org hierarch.  
02_Org_ Hierarchy_Report_Detail.xlsx 

Additional Location Information:
-	There were custom modifications to the item list search in RMS. In the new system we will still need the ability to make location lists and have security attached to who is making the lists.  Users need to be able to enter locations one at a time or in mass.
-	Users need to be able to rebuild (manually or automatically) location lists in RMS based on store attributes to capture any changes. 
-	Need to be able to see and filter down within the organizational hierarchy.  

Exceptions: 
-	n/a

Issues/Limitations: 
-	There is a data quality issue in FMF.  The owner of the data is each individual store.  There is little trust in the data.  There is also no governance over the data.  There is no way to know if the data is accurate or not, until there are issues.  
-	There are not facility attributes that allow users to know details about a location including 110/220 voltage, demographics or other information that could be used in MD decisions and PAR allocations.
-	The lack of visibility to annex locations in RMS and the visibility only to the branch level attributes can cause MD to make incorrect decisions about product to the annex locations.
-	There is not a way to identify what change were made when the “last changed date” field updates or the Y id associated with the change.  
-	There is not currently an owner of FMF.  MD did have some oversight, but it might be moving to store ops in the near future.  
-	New traits and other updates to the FMF require IT involvement, take considerable time and are challenging.
-	The eCommerce team maintains additional store data independently of FMF. eCommerce business users manually maintain this additional facility data.

Need process definition:
-	There is not currently a process for data accuracy or compliance.  
-	There is not a defined process for store opening dates and needed data in FMF.  Resulting in missed t-logs, inability to accept credit cards and last-minute scrambling to ensure a smooth opening. 
-	There is not a defined process for store closing dates and data needed.  There is not a systematic way to confirm when a store should stop selling.  Product can also be sent to a store until the store close date is added.  A lot of manual work goes into ensuring product is not shipped as a store is selling down.  
-	There is not a defined process for store name changes. 
-	Need ability to easily maintain org data for sister services accurately

Introduction
While teaching my year 7 class of 10 students with significant learning support needs, I found traditional methods were not effectively teaching abstract concepts like angles. So, I decided to take my students outside to the school greenhouse for a hands-on lesson. My plan involves having them identify angles within the greenhouse structure and use sticks to physically form different angles.
I chose this outdoor, kinaesthetic approach because it makes abstract concepts tangible and connects learning to the real world. Research supports this, indicating it enhances engagement and understanding, particularly for students who struggle with conventional methods (Abah et al., 2024). It also helps reduce maths anxiety and improves confidence by providing a less formal, more interactive environment (Grothérus & Fägerstam, 2018).
My interest in exploring alternative approaches like this stems from a commitment to making mathematics accessible and engaging for all learners, moving beyond rote learning towards more inclusive, experiential education that builds both skills and confidence (Nardi & Steward, 2003). This lesson was a practical step towards achieving that goal.
Literature Review
The literature reveals that mathematics learning beyond the classroom encompasses a wide range of contexts and approaches. Watson, Jones and Pratt (2013) identify several key avenues, including informal learning through games and puzzles, real-world applications, parental involvement, technology-enhanced learning, and cross-curricular connections. These varied approaches all contribute to developing mathematical thinking in contexts that may be more engaging and accessible than traditional classroom instruction.
One concerning finding comes from Nardi and Steward's (2003) study of Year 9 students, which reveals that homework is often perceived as an obligatory task driven by school and parental pressure rather than as an opportunity for meaningful engagement. Their research indicates that out-of-class learning frequently mirrors classroom issues, characterized by obligation and a focus on rote memorization. This suggests that simply extending classroom approaches to home settings may perpetuate disaffection rather than foster genuine interest.
In contrast, Morgan, Watson and Tikly (2004) emphasize the importance of recognizing the mathematical experiences students bring from their everyday lives. They highlight the value of community and cultural resources, outdoor environments, and information and communication technology in providing authentic and meaningful mathematical experiences. Their work suggests that leveraging these resources can help students see the relevance of mathematics beyond school settings.
This aligns with Lerman's (2014) discussion of informal learning in the Encyclopaedia of Mathematics Education, which defines it as the acquisition of mathematical knowledge outside of structured educational systems. Lerman identifies various sources of informal mathematical learning, including work-based learning, family and community activities, cultural practices, and early childhood learning through play. He argues that these experiences are not merely practical but also contribute to conceptual understanding through participation in social contexts.
Mason's (2002) concept of a "conjecturing atmosphere" further develops this idea by emphasizing the importance of creating environments where learners feel supported in making and testing mathematical conjectures. His work on the "discipline of noticing" suggests that teachers should develop an "inner witness" to become more aware of students' mathematical thinking across contexts. This reflective practice enables educators to better connect classroom instruction with the diverse mathematical understandings that students bring from their everyday experiences.
Lesson plan and task
My objective was clear: for students to not only define but also actively identify and physically create acute, right, obtuse, and straight angles. To achieve this, I planned a lesson situated for the most part outdoors, utilizing the school greenhouse as a dynamic, real-world learning environment. The greenhouse itself provides an ideal setting, rich with structural examples of angles, allowing students to bridge the gap between theoretical definitions and tangible, observable reality, a pedagogical strategy strongly advocated by researchers like Boaler (2016) who emphasize connecting mathematics to practical applications.
The novelty of the setting can stimulate interest, while the natural context provides authentic examples far removed from worksheet exercises. By asking students to find a right angle in a window frame or an acute angle in a roof brace, I am directly connecting the mathematical terms to their physical manifestations, making the learning experience more meaningful and memorable.
Natural materials form the core of the creative activity, so I gathered an ample supply of sticks of varying lengths from the school grounds. For recording observations during the exploration phase, simple worksheets paired with clipboards were essential, enabling students to sketch or make notes easily while moving around. Although primarily focused on identification and creation, I had protractors on hand for a potential extension activity involving angle measurement. Safety, of course, is a non-negotiable aspect of outdoor learning. I provided gloves for handling sticks and, crucially, conducted a thorough pre-lesson inspection of the greenhouse and surrounding area to identify and mitigate any potential hazards, such as uneven ground, sharp edges, or damaged structures.
The lesson begun with a focused 10-minute introduction right outside the greenhouse. Gathering the students, I clearly articulated the lesson's goals and briefly reviewed the definitions of acute (<90°), right (90°), obtuse (>90°), and straight (180°) angles, using accessible language and quick physical demonstrations. I then modelled the first activity by pointing out clear examples of these angles within the greenhouse structure itself. Simultaneously, the Teaching Assistant (TA) distributed the necessary worksheets and clipboards, ensuring every student was ready and understood the initial task.
The first activity, lasted roughly 15 minutes, involved students working collaboratively in pairs to explore the greenhouse environment. Their mission was to actively locate and identify different types of angles within the building's structure – beams, window frames, support struts, roof pitches etc. Each pair needed to find and record, through sketches or descriptions, at least one example of an acute, right, and obtuse angle. During this exploration, my role was to oversee the activity, gauge overall understanding, and facilitate learning, while the TA provided crucial support by circulating among the pairs, assisting those who are struggling, reinforcing safety guidelines, and managing any minor behavioural issues discreetly.
Next, we transitioned into the 20-minute creation phase. I distributed the sticks. Still in their pairs, students used the sticks to physically construct their own examples of acute, right, and obtuse angles on the ground or another suitable surface. The emphasis here was on experimentation and manipulation. I circulated to pose questions, checked for understanding, and encouraged discussion within pairs, while the TA focused on providing more intensive support to any groups needing extra help, ensuring everyone participated actively.
To consolidate the learning, a 10-minute plenary discussion followed in the classroom. I guided a whole-group conversation, inviting pairs to share specific angles they found or created. Facilitative questions like, "Which type of angle was hardest to find/make?" or "How did physically making the angle help you remember its name?" aim to deepen reflection and verbalise their understanding. 
References
Abah, J., Chinaka, T.W. and Ogbiji, E.O., 2024. Effect of Kinesthetic Learning on Students’ Interest and Achievement in Mathematics. Mathematics Education Journal, 8(2), pp.120-136.
Boaler, J. (2016) Mathematical Mindsets: Unleashing Students' Potential Through Creative Math, Inspiring Messages and Innovative Teaching. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.
Grothérus, A. and Fägerstam, E., 2018. Lower secondary students' experiences of outdoor learning in mathematics – impact on self-regulation and mathematical proficiency. Available at: Outdoor Learning [Accessed 16 April 2025].
Lerman, S. (2014): Encyclopedia of mathematics education. Dordrecht: Springer. 
Mason, J. (2002): Researching Your Own Practice: The discipline of noticing. London: Routledge
Morgan, C., Watson, A. & Tikly, C. (2004): Teaching School Subjects 11-19: Mathematics. London: Routledge.
Nardi, E. & Steward, S. (2003) Is mathematics T.I.R.E.D.? A profile of quiet disaffection in the secondary mathematics classroom. British Educational Research Journal, 29(3), pp. 345-367.
Watson, P., Jones, K. & Pratt, D. (2013): Key ideas in teaching mathematics: Research-based guidance for ages 9-19. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

I chose this outdoor, kinaesthetic approach because it makes abstract concepts tangible and connects learning to the real world. Research supports this, indicating it enhances engagement and understanding, particularly for students who struggle with conventional methods (Abah et al., 2024). It also helps reduce maths anxiety and improves confidence by providing a less formal, more interactive environment (Grothérus & Fägerstam, 2018).
My interest in exploring alternative approaches like this stems from a commitment to making mathematics accessible and engaging for all learners, moving beyond rote learning towards more inclusive, experiential education that builds both skills and confidence (Nardi & Steward, 2003). This lesson was a practical step towards achieving that goal.
Literature Review
The literature reveals that mathematics learning beyond the classroom encompasses a wide range of contexts and approaches. Watson, Jones and Pratt (2013) identify several key avenues, including informal learning through games and puzzles, real-world applications, parental involvement, technology-enhanced learning, and cross-curricular connections. These varied approaches all contribute to developing mathematical thinking in contexts that may be more engaging and accessible than traditional classroom instruction.
One concerning finding comes from Nardi and Steward's (2003) study of Year 9 students, which reveals that homework is often perceived as an obligatory task driven by school and parental pressure rather than as an opportunity for meaningful engagement. Their research indicates that out-of-class learning frequently mirrors classroom issues, characterized by obligation and a focus on rote memorization. This suggests that simply extending classroom approaches to home settings may perpetuate disaffection rather than foster genuine interest.
In contrast, Morgan, Watson and Tikly (2004) emphasize the importance of recognizing the mathematical experiences students bring from their everyday lives. They highlight the value of community and cultural resources, outdoor environments, and information and communication technology in providing authentic and meaningful mathematical experiences. Their work suggests that leveraging these resources can help students see the relevance of mathematics beyond school settings.
This aligns with Lerman's (2014) discussion of informal learning in the Encyclopaedia of Mathematics Education, which defines it as the acquisition of mathematical knowledge outside of structured educational systems. Lerman identifies various sources of informal mathematical learning, including work-based learning, family and community activities, cultural practices, and early childhood learning through play. He argues that these experiences are not merely practical but also contribute to conceptual understanding through participation in social contexts.
Mason's (2002) concept of a "conjecturing atmosphere" further develops this idea by emphasizing the importance of creating environments where learners feel supported in making and testing mathematical conjectures. His work on the "discipline of noticing" suggests that teachers should develop an "inner witness" to become more aware of students' mathematical thinking across contexts. This reflective practice enables educators to better connect classroom instruction with the diverse mathematical understandings that students bring from their everyday experiences.
Lesson plan and task
My objective was clear: for students to not only define but also actively identify and physically create acute, right, obtuse, and straight angles. To achieve this, I planned a lesson situated for the most part outdoors, utilizing the school greenhouse as a dynamic, real-world learning environment. The greenhouse itself provides an ideal setting, rich with structural examples of angles, allowing students to bridge the gap between theoretical definitions and tangible, observable reality, a pedagogical strategy strongly advocated by researchers like Boaler (2016) who emphasize connecting mathematics to practical applications.
The novelty of the setting can stimulate interest, while the natural context provides authentic examples far removed from worksheet exercises. By asking students to find a right angle in a window frame or an acute angle in a roof brace, I am directly connecting the mathematical terms to their physical manifestations, making the learning experience more meaningful and memorable.
Natural materials form the core of the creative activity, so I gathered an ample supply of sticks of varying lengths from the school grounds. For recording observations during the exploration phase, simple worksheets paired with clipboards were essential, enabling students to sketch or make notes easily while moving around. Although primarily focused on identification and creation, I had protractors on hand for a potential extension activity involving angle measurement. Safety, of course, is a non-negotiable aspect of outdoor learning. I provided gloves for handling sticks and, crucially, conducted a thorough pre-lesson inspection of the greenhouse and surrounding area to identify and mitigate any potential hazards, such as uneven ground, sharp edges, or damaged structures.
The lesson begun with a focused 10-minute introduction right outside the greenhouse. Gathering the students, I clearly articulated the lesson's goals and briefly reviewed the definitions of acute (<90°), right (90°), obtuse (>90°), and straight (180°) angles, using accessible language and quick physical demonstrations. I then modelled the first activity by pointing out clear examples of these angles within the greenhouse structure itself. Simultaneously, the Teaching Assistant (TA) distributed the necessary worksheets and clipboards, ensuring every student was ready and understood the initial task.
The first activity, lasted roughly 15 minutes, involved students working collaboratively in pairs to explore the greenhouse environment. Their mission was to actively locate and identify different types of angles within the building's structure – beams, window frames, support struts, roof pitches etc. Each pair needed to find and record, through sketches or descriptions, at least one example of an acute, right, and obtuse angle. During this exploration, my role was to oversee the activity, gauge overall understanding, and facilitate learning, while the TA provided crucial support by circulating among the pairs, assisting those who are struggling, reinforcing safety guidelines, and managing any minor behavioural issues discreetly.
Next, we transitioned into the 20-minute creation phase. I distributed the sticks. Still in their pairs, students used the sticks to physically construct their own examples of acute, right, and obtuse angles on the ground or another suitable surface. The emphasis here was on experimentation and manipulation. I circulated to pose questions, checked for understanding, and encouraged discussion within pairs, while the TA focused on providing more intensive support to any groups needing extra help, ensuring everyone participated actively.
To consolidate the learning, a 10-minute plenary discussion followed in the classroom. I guided a whole-group conversation, inviting pairs to share specific angles they found or created. Facilitative questions like, "Which type of angle was hardest to find/make?" or "How did physically making the angle help you remember its name?" aim to deepen reflection and verbalise their understanding.

História e Evolução do Jogo da Forca
A história do Jogo da Forca remonta a séculos atrás, sendo uma forma popular de entretenimento que transcendeu culturas e continentes. Embora sua origem exata seja incerta, algumas teorias sugerem que o jogo pode ter surgido na Grécia Antiga, onde era chamado de "Jogo de Palavras". No entanto, o jogo como o conhecemos hoje ganhou destaque na Europa durante a Idade Média.

Durante esse período, o Jogo da Forca era frequentemente praticado em tavernas e praças públicas, desafiando a habilidade dos jogadores em adivinhar palavras ocultas. O desenho da forca em si, com seu aspecto enigmático e sombrio, adicionava uma dose extra de suspense ao jogo. À medida que o tempo passou, o Jogo da Forca se espalhou pelo mundo e sofreu diversas adaptações e evoluções, sendo incorporado a diferentes culturas e idiomas.

Atualmente, com a popularização da tecnologia, o Jogo da Forca também encontrou seu espaço no mundo virtual. Ele pode ser jogado online em diversos sites e aplicativos, proporcionando uma experiência interativa e divertida para jogadores de todas as idades. Apesar das mudanças ao longo dos anos, a essência do Jogo da Forca permanece a mesma: um desafio intelectual que estimula o raciocínio, o vocabulário e a diversão entre os participantes.

Benefícios Educacionais do Jogo da Forca
O Jogo da Forca oferece uma série de benefícios educacionais, tornando-o uma ferramenta valiosa para o desenvolvimento do vocabulário e habilidades linguísticas. Primeiramente, o jogo ajuda a expandir o conhecimento de palavras, permitindo que os jogadores aprendam novos termos e expressem suas ideias de maneira mais precisa. A exposição a diferentes palavras e suas definições contribui para o enriquecimento do vocabulário.

Além disso, o Jogo da Forca estimula o raciocínio lógico e a dedução. Os jogadores precisam pensar estrategicamente, considerando as letras disponíveis, as palavras já tentadas e as dicas fornecidas. Isso desenvolve habilidades de resolução de problemas, estimula a criatividade e promove a capacidade de análise e síntese de informações.

Outro benefício é o estímulo à interação social e ao trabalho em equipe. O Jogo da Forca pode ser jogado em grupo, incentivando a colaboração e a comunicação entre os participantes. Essa interação promove a troca de conhecimentos, a construção coletiva de soluções e fortalece os laços interpessoais.

Em suma, o Jogo da Forca vai além de ser apenas uma diversão. Ele se mostra uma ferramenta educacional eficaz, auxiliando no desenvolvimento do vocabulário, no estímulo ao raciocínio lógico e na promoção da interação social. Seja em sala de aula, em casa ou em ambientes virtuais, o Jogo da Forca pode ser aproveitado como uma maneira envolvente e eficiente de aprendizado.
